content.title: Virginia DUI Laws, Penalties and Defenses § 18.2-266 Explained by DWI Attorney for Alexandria, Fairfax, Arlington
content.text: Virginia DUI / DWI Charges – VA Code § 18.2-266Under Virginia law, a DUI or a DWI is a serious criminal offense that is punished as a misdemeanor or a felony under Virginia Law § 18.2-266, depending on the number of prior drunk driving convictions. (DUI and DWI can be used interchangeably in Virginia).A first offense DUI is a Class 1 misdemeanor punished by up to 12 months in jail, a fine ranging from $250 to $2,500, 12 months of driver’s license suspension, and mandatory alcohol program participation. If the blood alcohol content was 0.15 or higher, mandatory minimum jail term of 5 days is enforced. A second DWI offense carries a mandatory jail term of at least 10 days and a fine of at least $500. With each aggravating factor as shown in the chart below, the mandatory minimum jail time increases. A third or subsequent DWI offense is treated as a felony punished by up to 5 years in prison and permanent revocation of driving privileges.Virginia’s strict enforcement of DUI laws means that even a first offense can have lasting impacts on your employment, criminal record and driving privileges. If you’re facing a DWI charge, it’s crucial to consult with an experienced Virginia DWI attorney to navigate the legal process and protect your rights.This article is written by a top-rated drunk driving defense lawyer who represents clients charged with DUI and DWI offenses in Northern Virginia – Arlington, Fairfax, and Alexandria.Virginia DUI / DWI Penalties ExplainedIn Virginia, DUI / DWI offenses are classified as misdemeanors or felonies depending on the number of prior convictions, and penalties increase significantly with higher blood alcohol content (BAC) and with each subsequent offense.A first offense DWI is a Class 1 misdemeanor punishable by up to 12 months in jail, a fine ranging from $250 to $2,500, and a 12-month license suspension. There is no mandatory minimum jail time unless the driver’s BAC is elevated. A BAC of 0.15 or higher results in a 5-day mandatory minimum, and a BAC over 0.20 increases the mandatory minimum to 10 days.A second DWI offense within 10 years remains a misdemeanor and is punishable by up to 12 months in jail, with a mandatory minimum of 10 days. If the BAC is 0.15 or higher, the minimum becomes 20 days, and if over 0.20, the minimum is 30 days. Fines range from $500 to $2,500, and the license suspension period is 36 months. If the second offense occurs within 5 years, the penalties are steeper, with a mandatory minimum of 20 days in jail, increasing to 30 days for a BAC of 0.15 or higher, and 40 days for a BAC above 0.20. The fine and license loss remain the same as those for a second offense in 10 years.A third DWI offense within 10 years is classified as a felony, punishable by up to 5 years in prison, with a mandatory minimum of 90 days, or 100 days if BAC is 0.15 or higher, and 110 days if BAC exceeds 0.20. The fine ranges from $1,000 to $2,500, and the offender’s driver’s license will be revoked indefinitely. For a third offense within 5 years, the mandatory minimum jail time is 180 days, rising to 190 days for a BAC of 0.15 or higher, and 200 days for BAC over 0.20. The fine and indefinite license revocation remain the same.A fourth DWI offense within 10 years is also a felony with a maximum sentence of 5 years in prison and a mandatory minimum jail sentence of 1 year, regardless of BAC. The fine is between $1,000 and $2,500, and the driver’s license will be revoked indefinitely.In addition to these penalties, driving under the influence with a child passenger—defined as anyone 17 years old or younger—results in enhanced DUI penalties. A first offense includes an additional fine ranging from $500 to $1,000 and an additional mandatory minimum jail sentence of 5 days, which must be served consecutively with any other DUI-related jail time. For a second offense, 80 hours of community service benefiting children is added on to the jail and fine penalties.Virginia DUI and DWI Penalty TableDUI OffenseClassificationMax. JailMin. JailMin. Virginia Code § 18.2-266 covers all drunk driving offenses under a single statue: DUI (Driving Under the Influence), DWI (Driving While Intoxicated), and DUID (Driving Under the Influence of Drugs). DUI penalties vary based on the number of prior offenses and the driver’s BAC level. Since they are punished in the same way and under the same statute, we use the terms DUI and DWI interchangeably.Importantly, Virginia law does not require a BAC of 0.08% or higher to convict a person of DUI. While most cases do involve a BAC at or above that threshold, you can still be arrested and convicted for DUI with a BAC below 0.08% if the officer believes your driving behavior indicates impairment. The statute allows prosecution for being “under the influence” based on totality of circumstances, not just a chemical reading.A first-time DUI offense in Virginia is a serious criminal charge and often a wake-up call for clients who may be familiar with more lenient procedures in other states. Unlike Maryland, which allows first-time dismissals, or jurisdictions that routinely reduce charges to reckless driving, Northern Virginia courts rarely offer such leniency. Virginia does not offer a first-offender diversion program. First Offense DUI charges become criminal convictions that are reported to the Central Criminal Records Exchange, creating a permanent criminal record that can impact employment, security clearances, and professional licensing.Furthermore, an arrest alone triggers immediate administrative license suspension—even before your court date. A first offense results in a 7-day license suspension, a second offense leads to a 60-day suspension, and a third or subsequent offense results in an indefinite suspension until trial.Northern Virginia jurisdictions— Alexandria, Arlington, and Fairfax —strictly enforce Virginia’s DUI and DWI laws as outlined in Va. Code § 18.2-266, applying the full extent of the penalties permitted under state law. These localities are known for their zero-tolerance approach to impaired driving, and individuals charged with a DUI often face some of the harshest consequences in the country.In short, Virginia takes impaired driving extremely seriously, and Northern Virginia enforces those laws aggressively. Anyone charged with a DUI in Alexandria, Arlington, or Fairfax should seek the services of an experienced DWI defense attorney. Prosecutors often rely on driving behavior, field sobriety tests, preliminary breath tests, video recording, officer observations, and breathalyzer or blood test results, all of which are vulnerable to challenges regarding accuracy, administration, and law enforcement procedures. A skilled lawyer will scrutinize whether the stop was lawful, whether probable cause existed, and whether the evidence meets Virginia’s strict standards.Sometimes a case simply has no defense under the law. This is more common than not. In such circumstances, a strong defense lawyer will be negotiating for mitigation to reduce your charge or penalties, or even seek dropped or dismissed charges in certain circumstances. Do not despair – speak to a lawyer to better understand your realistic penalty potentials.If you have been charged with DUI in Northern Virginia, contact MEDVIN LAW to protect your rights, minimize penalties and consequences, and be represented by an attorney concentrated on securing your most favorable result. We defend DUI and DWI cases in Fairfax, Arlington, Alexandria, Falls Church, and Vienna.How BAC Levels Shape DWI Defense in VirginiaVirginia’s DWI laws significantly limit defense strategies when a Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) level is involved, shifting the legal landscape in ways that differ sharply from most other criminal cases.In typical criminal proceedings, the burden of proof rests entirely on the government to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. However, in Virginia DWI cases, that standard shifts when your BAC is 0.08% or higher. At that threshold, Virginia law imposes a legal presumption of intoxication—meaning the court will presume that you were under the influence at the time of the offense. When you walk into court with a DWI charge and a BAC of 0.08 or above, you are already presumed guilty of driving under the influence unless you and your attorney can successfully rebut that presumption.If your BAC falls between 0.05 and 0.08, there is no legal presumption either way. In these cases, the prosecution must prove impairment beyond a reasonable doubt, relying on other evidence such as driving behavior, field sobriety tests, and officer observations.When the BAC is 0.05 or below, the law creates a presumption that the driver was not under the influence, restoring the standard presumption of innocence. In such cases, the burden shifts back to the Commonwealth to prove intoxication through additional evidence, often a challenging task for prosecutors.This structure—where presumptions based on BAC levels effectively shift the burden of proof away from the prosecution—is what makes Virginia’s DUI laws especially harsh. Defending a DWI case in this framework requires careful legal strategy, expert understanding of the science behind BAC readings, and aggressive courtroom advocacy.Adding to the severity, Virginia treats DUI and DWI offenses as criminal misdemeanors, not just traffic violations. While some states may view a first offense DUI as a civil infraction or allow routine reductions to “wet reckless” charges, Virginia imposes strict criminal penalties. Even Reckless Driving, often used as a plea alternative in other states, is itself a Class 1 misdemeanor in Virginia, codified within the state’s traffic code but carrying the same criminal weight.In short, BAC levels not only influence how DUI cases are prosecuted—they often dictate the legal hurdles a defendant must overcome. If you’re facing a DWI charge in Virginia you need a defense attorney who understands how to challenge the presumptions, question the evidence, and present a compelling defense.Virginia Drunk Driving Penalties OutlinedFirst Offense DUI / DWI PenaltiesMaximum Penalties DUI 1st(1) up to 1 year in jail, (2) mandatory minimum jail sentence for certain BAC levels and case facts (3) up to an indefinite suspension of your driver’s license/privileges, (4) ignition interlock device for your vehicle if you get a restricted license at your expense, (5) completion of ASAP (Alcohol Safety & Awareness Program) at your expense, (6) a total of 6 points on a Virginia driver’s license, and, (7) between a $250.00 and $2,500.00 fine.Minimum Penalties DUI 1st1) you must attend ASAP classes at your expense 2) your driver’s license will be suspended for a period of 12 months 3) if your BAC level was between .15-.20, you MUST serve at least 5 days in jail 4) if your BAC level was above .20, you MUST serve at least 10 days in jail 5) if you had a child passenger in your vehicle at the time of the offense who was under the age of 18 at the time, you MUST serve at least 5 days in jail – with an additional fine between $500.00 and $1,000.00Second Offense DUI / DWI PenaltiesMin. Law enforcement officers are trained to observe specific driving behaviors that may indicate impairment, and once a stop is made, the investigation intensifies through observations, questioning, and roadside testing. Understanding what officers look for during a DUI stop can help you recognize how cases are built—and where legal defenses may apply.Driving Behaviors That Trigger DUI StopsVirginia police officers are trained to identify driving patterns associated with intoxication. These behaviors typically fall into four categories:Lane Position ProblemsDrivers suspected of DWI often struggle to maintain proper lane control. Common cues include:• Weaving or drifting across lane lines• Straddling a lane divider• Swerving or making wide, exaggerated turns• Nearly hitting vehicles, curbs, or roadside objects• Stopping too far from a curb or at an odd angle• Abrupt, jerky stops or stopping beyond the limit lineVigilance and Awareness FailuresImpaired drivers often show signs of diminished awareness or attention to surroundings:• Driving the wrong way on a one-way street or into opposing lanes• Failing to respond promptly to traffic signals or signs• Ignoring signals from the officer• Stopping unexpectedly or without a clear reason• Driving at night without headlights• Failing to signal or using signals improperlySpeed and Braking IssuesErratic changes in speed and poor braking control are also red flags for impairment:• Unexplained acceleration or deceleration• Inconsistent speed maintenance• Stopping too abruptly or not enough• Driving significantly below the speed limit (10+ mph under)Judgment and Decision-Making ErrorsAlcohol and drug impairment affects a driver’s ability to make safe decisions:• Following other vehicles too closely• Making unsafe or illegal lane changes• Taking sharp or erratic turns• Failing to stay on designated roadways• Odd behavior in response to an officer’s commands• Throwing objects from the vehicle or engaging in argumentative behavior• Displaying visible signs of intoxicationPost-Stop Observations Used in DWI CasesAfter stopping a driver, officers continue evaluating for signs of intoxication. These observations are often documented in police reports and used as evidence in court. Key post-stop indicators include:• Difficulty using basic vehicle controls• Trouble exiting the vehicle safely or steadily• Fumbling with license or registration• Repetitive or irrelevant speech• Noticeable balance issues, swaying, or leaning for support• Slurred speech and poor coordination• Delayed response to questions or commands• Inconsistent answers or incorrect personal information• The odor of alcohol coming from the driverPolice officers rely heavily on these behavioral cues and physical signs to justify a DUI arrest and to support their findings in court. However, not all observed behaviors are the result of intoxication—medical conditions, fatigue, or nervousness can mimic impairment. That is why an experienced DUI defense attorney is critical to review the facts, challenge assumptions, and build a defense tailored to the specifics of your case.Field Sobriety TestsIn most DUI stops, Virginia police officers initially lack sufficient evidence to arrest a driver while the individual remains in the vehicle. To develop probable cause, officers typically ask the driver to step out and submit to a series of field sobriety tests (FSTs). These tests are voluntary—Virginia law does not require drivers to perform them—but many individuals comply, mistakenly believing cooperation may help their case. Unfortunately, performing these tests often provides officers with incriminating evidence they would not otherwise have, and in many cases, can establish the basis for arrest.Horizontal Gaze Nystagmus (HGN) TestThe HGN test examines the involuntary jerking of the eyes—known as nystagmus—that becomes more pronounced when a person is impaired by alcohol. During the test, the officer asks the subject to follow a pen or small flashlight with their eyes while observing for three key indicators in each eye:• Lack of smooth pursuit• Distinct jerking at maximum deviation• Onset of jerking within 45 degrees of centerIf four or more indicators are present, officers are trained to believe the driver’s BAC is likely 0.08 or higher. However, HGN results can be affected by other factors, including seizure medications, inhalants, barbiturates, and certain medical conditions, raising questions about reliability.One-Leg Stand TestIn the One-Leg Stand, the driver must lift one foot approximately six inches off the ground and count aloud for 30 seconds. Officers look for four signs of impairment:• Swaying while balancing• Using arms for balance• Hopping• Putting the foot down before instructedWalk-and-Turn TestThe Walk-and-Turn is a divided-attention test that challenges both mental focus and physical coordination. The subject must take nine heel-to-toe steps in a straight line, turn using a specific pivot motion, and return the same way. Indicators of impairment include:• Failing to maintain balance during instructions• Starting before being told• Stopping mid-walk• Stepping off the line• Using arms for balance• Making an improper turn• Taking the incorrect number of stepsEven sober individuals may struggle with this test, especially under stress, on uneven pavement, or in poor weather.Preliminary Breath TestVirginia police officers offer a voluntary preliminary breath test and make arrest decisions based on the reading of the PBT device.• A BAC reading of .08 or greater on the PBT test will result in probable cause for an arrestBreath and Blood Tests in DUI CasesAfter a DUI arrest, Virginia police will ask the driver to submit to a breath or blood test to measure Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC). If a driver refuses, officers can charge Refusal and seek a warrant to compel a blood test.Per Virginia’s implied consent law, anyone who operates a vehicle on Virginia roads automatically consents to a chemical test of their breath or blood if arrested for DUI, provided the arrest takes place within three hours of the alleged DWI (the time of driving or operation).Refusal to submit to breath or blood testing is an independent violation of law, in addition to the DWI charge. All Refusal license suspension periods run consecutively, not concurrently, with the DUI charge penalties.Virginia Law on Refusal of Breath or Blood Test Following DWI / DUI Arrest – VA Code § 18.2-268.3Virginia DUI / DWI Police Investigation ChartOperating a Vehicle in a Virginia DUI Case: What It Means to Be Behind the WheelUnder Virginia DUI law, you do not need to be actively driving a vehicle to be charged with Driving Under the Influence (DUI). The Virginia Code defines an “operator” or “driver” as “every person who either (i) drives or is in actual physical control of a motor vehicle on a highway or (ii) is exercising control over or steering a vehicle being towed by a motor vehicle.” This broad definition allows law enforcement and courts to interpret “operation” more expansively than simply driving.The Virginia Supreme Court has made clear that any person in actual physical control of a vehicle qualifies as an operator, even if the vehicle is not moving. Courts have consistently upheld that an intoxicated individual sitting behind the steering wheel of a vehicle on a public highway, with the key in the ignition, is legally considered to be operating the vehicle within the meaning of Va. Code § 18.2-266—and is therefore subject to DUI charges.As a result, Virginia law allows for DUI arrests even when the vehicle is stationary. Common scenarios where individuals have been charged include:• Sitting in the driver’s seat of a parked vehicle with the engine running • Sleeping behind the wheel with the keys in the ignition • Listening to the radio while seated in the driver’s seat with the vehicle on • Having the keys in your lap or within easy reach while in the driver’s seatThe rationale behind this interpretation is to prevent individuals from becoming a danger to the public the moment they decide to drive, especially while impaired. In practical terms, this means that Virginia police officers can and often do charge DUI suspects who are not actively driving, but who are perceived to be capable of doing so.Because the definition of “operation” is interpreted so broadly in Virginia DUI law, it’s important to understand that physical presence in the driver’s seat with access to the ignition may be enough to support a DUI arrest. If you’ve been charged with DUI under these circumstances, it is critical to consult with an experienced DUI defense attorney who can challenge whether the Commonwealth has sufficiently proven “operation” under the law.Comprehensive Guide to Federal DWI and DUI Crimes Prosecuted in Alexandria, VirginiaFederal DWI and DUI Laws and Penalties Applicable to Virginia Explained by Federal Criminal Defense Attorney
